nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

nodes.title: Automation and IaC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

nodes.title: Wan: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Wan. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A multi-site enterprise wants to: (a) decouple WAN policy from hardware vendor, (b) use multiple transports (MPLS + broadband + LTE) actively, (c) centralise policy (URL filtering, QoS, app routing) via a controller, (d) push intent-based config to branch CPEs. Which technology?
flashcards.back: SD-WAN (Cisco Viptela/SDWAN, VMware VeloCloud) centralizes WAN control, enables application-aware routing, automatic failover between WAN links, and reduces costs by using broadband/LTE alongside MPLS.

flashcards.front: Two routers need to encapsulate ANY Layer-3 protocol (IPv4, IPv6, IPX) inside an IP packet to traverse an intermediate network. The encapsulation adds a 4-byte protocol-id header and an outer IP header. The result LOOKS like an IP packet to the intermediate network but transparently carries the inner payload. Which tunnel?
flashcards.back: GRE (Protocol 47) wraps packets in an IP + GRE header, allowing non-IP protocols or multicast over IP networks. GRE itself provides no encryption — combine with IPSec for secure tunnels. Used in DMVPN and SD-WAN. encapsulates virtually any Layer 3 protocol inside IP packets, creating a virtual point-to-point tunnel between endpoints across IP networks

flashcards.front: A hub-and-spoke WAN with 500 branch offices needs spoke-to-spoke dynamic tunnels (without the hub in the data path) WITHOUT pre-configuring every spoke pair. The Cisco solution combines GRE multipoint (mGRE), NHRP for next-hop resolution, and IPsec for encryption. What is this technology?
flashcards.back: DMVPN phases: Phase 1 (hub-and-spoke, all traffic through hub), Phase 2 (spoke-to-spoke direct tunnels, no summarization), Phase 3 (spoke-to-spoke with summarization via NHRP redirect). Reduces hub load.

flashcards.front: In DMVPN Phase 2 / 3, a SPOKE wants to talk directly to another SPOKE (not via the hub). It needs to discover the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a dynamic mapping table; spokes query it on demand. Which protocol?
flashcards.back: In DMVPN, NHRP allows spoke routers to query the hub for the physical (NBMA) address of other spokes, enabling on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels without pre-configuring all pairs. Hub maintains NHRP database.

nodes.title: Campus: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Campus. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Cisco's campus network architecture uses: VXLAN overlay fabric, LISP for the overlay control plane, ISE for identity-based policy (SGT tags), and DNA Center for orchestration. Endpoints get a scalable group tag (SGT) and policy is enforced uniformly. What is this called?
flashcards.back: SD-Access: Underlay (routed access), Overlay (VXLAN/LISP), Policy (ISE+SGT/SGACLs), Management (DNA Center). Virtual Networks (VNs) provide macro-segmentation; Scalable Group Tags (SGTs) provide micro-segmentation.

flashcards.front: Cisco SD-Access uses a control-plane protocol that separates an endpoint's IDENTITY (Endpoint Identifier, EID) from its LOCATION (Routing Locator, RLOC). When an EID moves to a new RLOC (host mobility), the control plane updates the mapping without changing the IP address. Which protocol?
flashcards.back: LISP maps EIDs to RLOCs via a Map-Server/Map-Resolver. When a host moves, only the LISP map changes, not the routing table. In SD-Access, LISP distributes host-to-switch-location mappings across the fabric. IP/MAC) from its location (RLOC — routing locator) — enables mobility without changing routing tables. Used as overlay control plane in Cisco SD-Access

flashcards.front: Cisco SD-Access uses two complementary segmentation constructs. (A) MACRO segmentation — entire routing domain (VRF-lite-style), separating tenants. (B) MICRO segmentation — 16-bit tag attached to users/devices by ISE; enforcement points compare tags via Cisco TrustSec. Which mapping?
flashcards.back: SD-Access segmentation: VNs (like VRFs) for isolation between major groups (IoT, Guest, Corp). Within a VN, SGTs (1-65535) tag users/endpoints by role. SGACLs (Cisco TrustSec) enforce which SGTs can communicate.

flashcards.front: In LISP, every packet to a new EID would normally trigger a Map-Request to the Map Server. Sub-second performance requires caching the EID-to-RLOC binding LOCALLY at the LISP router so subsequent packets to the same destination skip the lookup. What is this?
flashcards.back: LISP first packet: ITR sends Map-Request to Map-Resolver → Map-Server → responds with RLOC. ITR caches EID→RLOC mapping. Subsequent packets: encapsulate directly using cached RLOC. Map-Cache: show lisp site / show lisp map-cache.

nodes.title: Amazon VPC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPC is a logically isolated network inside an AWS region. You define the IP range, create subnets in multiple AZs, route tables decide where packets go, and security groups + NACLs filter what's allowed. Most networking exam Qs are VPC-shaped.

flashcards.front: Public vs private subnet — what makes the difference?
flashcards.back: Routing. A 'public' subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW). A 'private' subnet doesn't — its instances can reach the internet only via a NAT Gateway (outbound) or VPC endpoint (to specific AWS services). The subnet's CIDR doesn't determine its category — the route table does.

flashcards.front: Security group vs network ACL — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Security group: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), applied per ENI / instance, default deny, allow rules only. NACL: stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly), applied per subnet, supports allow and deny rules, evaluated in numbered order. SGs handle 95% of cases; NACLs add a deny-list at the subnet edge.

flashcards.front: What's a NAT Gateway for?
flashcards.back: Lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound internet traffic (package updates, API calls to public endpoints) while remaining unreachable from the internet. The NAT replaces the source IP with its own elastic IP. One per AZ for HA — they're zonal, not regional.

flashcards.front: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway — when to scale up?
flashcards.back: Peering connects two VPCs (mesh: N VPCs need N×(N-1)/2 peerings). It's free per-GB but doesn't transit. Transit Gateway is a hub: many VPCs and on-prem VPNs all connect to it, full transitive routing. Use peering up to ~5 VPCs; switch to TGW when the mesh becomes painful.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Mixed Topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Mixed Topics. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: Cisco ships THREE distinct OS lineages. (A) Modular IOS for enterprise routers and switches (ASR, ISR, Cat9k). (B) Carrier-grade high-availability OS for service-provider edge (ASR9k / NCS). (C) Linux-based DC OS for Nexus switches with VDCs and per-process restart. Which mapping is correct?
flashcards.back: IOS-XE: modular architecture (SPA/SIP separation), enterprise-grade. IOS-XR: microkernel, in-service software upgrade (ISSU), massive scale, 32-bit process separation. NX-OS: Linux-based, programmable, feature-rich for data center.

flashcards.front: A Cisco chassis with redundant Route Processors (RPs) maintains forwarding during an RP failover. The ACTIVE RP continuously syncs control-plane state (RIB, FIB, adjacencies, protocol state) to the STANDBY RP. On failover, the standby takes over in milliseconds with NO route flap (the FIB stays programmed). What's this feature pair?
flashcards.back: Without NSF/SSO: RP failure = routing restart = traffic loss during convergence. With SSO: standby RP fully synchronized, sub-second failover. With NSF: keeps forwarding during reconvergence. OSPF/BGP/EIGRP-aware NSF helpers exist.

flashcards.front: Cisco offers three multi-chassis switching constructs. (A) Stackwise — two or more access switches stack via physical cables, behave as one virtual switch (Cat 3750/3850/9300). (B) VSS — TWO Cat 6500/4500 chassis act as one logical switch (legacy DC core). (C) vPC — two Nexus switches present a port-channel jointly to a downstream device, but each has its OWN control plane. Which mapping?
flashcards.back: Stackwise: physical ring cable, 80Gbps backplane, 9 switches max, single management IP. VSS: active/standby supervisor, full mesh between chassis, geographic separation possible. vPC: most complex, fully independent management, data center focused.

flashcards.front: A network operator upgrades the IOS on a core router WITHOUT a maintenance window. Traffic must continue forwarding; routing protocol adjacencies must NOT flap. The operation requires: (a) redundant supervisors with NSF / SSO, (b) compatible OS versions side-by-side (forward+backward compat), (c) ISSU-aware feature image. What's this called?
flashcards.back: ISSU process: standby RP upgraded first, switchover (SSO), active RP upgraded, switchover back. Throughout: NSF maintains forwarding, SSO maintains protocol states. Requires: SSO configured, NSF for OSPF/BGP/EIGRP, ISSU-capable hardware, compatible versions.
